profile.name: La Danza
profile.insight: Composed by Rossini at a breakneck 152 dotted quarter notes per minute, this vocal patter song served as the melodic blueprint for the famous wedding tarantella 'C'è la luna mezzo mare'.
profile.profile: La Danza is an 1835 patter song composed by Gioachino Rossini in the rapid tempo of a Tarantella napoletana. Set to lyrics by Count Carlo Pepoli, it stands as the eighth piece in the collection Les soirées musicales. Originally intended for piano and bass voice, it functions as a stand-alone chamber piece rather than part of an opera. The composition became widely adapted by classical composers and remains celebrated globally through interpretations by major operatic vocalists.
profile.profile_long:
In the 1830s, Gioachino Rossini turned his creative focus toward sacred music, chamber music, and vocal compositions after stepping away from opera. Composed in 1835, 'La Danza' was written as the eighth piece in his twelve-song cycle 'Les soirées musicales' (1830–1835). Featuring Italian verses penned by Count Carlo Pepoli, who served as librettist for Vincenzo Bellini's opera 'I puritani', the song was conceived in a folk-character form. Rather than being embedded within an theatrical work, it was written as an independent vocal chamber piece originally intended with piano accompaniment for the bass singer Luigi Lablache.

Musically, Rossini structured the work as a patter song in 6/8 meter under the tempo marking Allegro con brio, calibrated at a metronome marking of 152 dotted quarter notes per minute. The composition opens with a 48-measure instrumental prelude before launching into its vocal text with the words 'Già la luna è in mezzo al mare...'. After an initial 60-measure section, it breaks into a 17-measure refrain of 'La! la ra la ra' in A major, recurring again after an eight-measure instrumental interlude and a second stanza starting with 'Salta, salta, gira, gira...'. Performers typically complete the piece in two to three minutes, with recorded tempos ranging from Enrico Caruso's 1912 rendition at three minutes and ten seconds to Cecilia Bartoli's rapid 2003 concert performance at two minutes and thirteen seconds.

Although fundamentally a musical work rather than a documented choreographic system, 'La Danza' takes its rhythmic vitality and structural spirit directly from the Tarantella napoletana. While the sources provide no step-by-step choreographic manuals or dance steps, its driving cadence has crossed into concert dance and popular culture. Franz Liszt arranged a virtuosic solo piano version in 1838, Frédéric Chopin drew inspiration from it for his Tarantelle in A-flat major, Op. 43, and Ottorino Respighi integrated an orchestral setting of the piece into the 1918 ballet 'La Boutique fantasque'. Furthermore, it served as a loose origin for the widely recognized Neapolitan wedding tarantella 'C'è la luna mezzo mare' and its subsequent English versions.

sections.origins_and_history: La Danza was composed in 1835 by Gioachino Rossini as part of 'Les soirées musicales', a twelve-piece collection created between 1830 and 1835. Rossini developed these folk-inflected chamber songs during a period when he stepped away from opera. The text was penned by Count Carlo Pepoli, who wrote the libretto for Bellini's 'I puritani'. The work was initially intended with piano accompaniment for the operatic bass Luigi Lablache.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. The provided sources describe 'La Danza' entirely as a vocal and instrumental musical composition in Tarantella napoletana time, containing no movement syllabus, dancer formations, or choreographic directions.
sections.music_and_instruments: Composed in 6/8 time with a minor key beginning and an Allegro con brio tempo of 152 dotted quarter notes per minute, the piece was originally scored for solo voice and piano. It features a 48-measure instrumental introduction, rapid vocal patter, and a repeated 17-measure refrain in A major on the syllables 'La! la ra la ra'. It has subsequently been transcribed for solo piano, chamber ensembles, and full orchestra.
sections.costume_and_setting: Sources do not describe folk costumes or staging traditions. Performances documented in sources occur primarily on classical concert stages, recording studios, and recital halls, including venues like the Teatro Lírico de Milano and the Teatro del Silenzio di Lajatico.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Conceived as a stand-alone vocal chamber piece for salon and concert performance, the piece channels the character of the Neapolitan tarantella. Beyond classical concerts, its melodic motifs loosely inspired the folk wedding song 'C'è la luna mezzo mare' and its English adaptations.
sections.notable_figures: The song was composed by Gioachino Rossini to lyrics by Count Carlo Pepoli, and originally conceived for the bass Luigi Lablache. In the nineteenth century, it was transcribed by Franz Liszt, Charles-Valentin Alkan, and Georges Cziffra, and inspired works by Frédéric Chopin and Ottorino Respighi. Celebrated twentieth- and twenty-first-century vocal performers include Enrico Caruso, Mario Lanza, Alfredo Kraus, Luciano Pavarotti, Andrea Bocelli, Juan Diego Flórez, Ramón Vargas, and Cecilia Bartoli.
sections.regional_variants: Variants mentioned in sources are primarily musical adaptations, including the wedding tune 'C'è la luna mezzo mare' and the English-language versions 'Oh! Ma-Ma!' and 'Lazy Mary', as well as Frida Boccara's musical adaptation 'Rossini et Beaumarchais'.
sections.lineage: Rooted in the musical tradition of the Tarantella napoletana, 'La Danza' spawned multiple classical transcriptions—notably Liszt's 1838 piano transcription (S 424/9) and Respighi's 1918 score for the ballet 'La Boutique fantasque'.

teaching.rhythm: 6/8 time, Allegro con brio (152 dotted quarter notes per minute)
teaching.level_notes: Choreographic technique is not detailed in the provided sources; the work is documented as a musical composition and patter song in tarantella rhythm.

gaps: The sources describe 'La Danza' as a classical vocal patter song in tarantella rhythm rather than a dance form with distinct steps.
No choreographic patterns, dancer roles, footwork, or partner formations are described in the sources.
Costumes, traditional settings, and community ceremonial functions are absent from the provided musical and encyclopedic entries.

claims.text: La Danza was composed in 1835 by Gioachino Rossini as a patter song in Tarantella napoletana time.
claims.quote: "La danza" (Dance) (1835) is a patter song by Gioachino Rossini, in Tarantella napoletana time

claims.text: The song is the eighth piece from the collection Les soirées musicales, spanning 1830 to 1835.
claims.quote: the eighth song of the collection Les soirées musicales (1830–1835).

claims.text: The lyrics to La Danza were written by Count Carlo Pepoli, librettist of Vincenzo Bellini's opera I puritani.
claims.quote: The lyrics are by Count Carlo Pepoli (it), librettist of Vincenzo Bellini's opera I puritani.

claims.text: La Danza is an independent chamber vocal piece rather than part of an opera or larger stage work.
claims.quote: "La danza" is a stand-alone chamber vocal piece, rather than part of a larger work.

claims.text: Franz Liszt and Charles-Valentin Alkan both made piano transcriptions of La Danza.
claims.quote: Franz Liszt transcribed it for piano, and so did Charles-Valentin Alkan

claims.text: Frédéric Chopin used the song as inspiration for his Tarantelle in A-flat, Op. 43, while Ottorino Respighi featured it in La Boutique fantasque.
claims.quote: Frédéric Chopin used the song as inspiration for his Tarantelle in A-flat, Op. 43; and Ottorino Respighi featured it in La Boutique fantasque.

claims.text: The song loosely served as the origin of the wedding tarantella C'è la luna mezzo mare and its English adaptations.
claims.quote: "La danza" was loosely the original source of the popular wedding tarantella "C'è la luna mezzo mare" and its English versions "Oh! Ma-Ma!" and "Lazy Mary".

claims.text: Rossini originally intended the song with piano accompaniment for the operatic bass Luigi Lablache.
claims.quote: Destinée à l'origine, avec un accompagnement de piano, à la basse Luigi Lablache qui, à l'opéra, avait chanté avec succès nombre de rôles de Rossini

claims.text: Rossini marked the tempo of the piece as Allegro con brio, at 152 dotted quarter notes per minute.
claims.quote: ajoute l'indication de mouvement Allegro con brio, soit au métronome un rythme de 152 à la noire pointée.

claims.text: The composition is set entirely in 6/8 meter and opens with an instrumental introduction of 48 measures.
claims.quote: La mesure 6/8 traverse toute la pièce... Après une introduction instrumentale de 48 mesures, la mélodie commence avec « Già la luna è in mezzo al mare… »

claims.text: Enrico Caruso recorded the piece in 1912 in three minutes and ten seconds.
claims.quote: Le ténor Enrico Caruso a chanté la chanson en 1912 dans un studio d'enregistrement en trois minutes et dix secondes.

claims.text: Cecilia Bartoli and conductor Myung-Whun Chung performed the piece in two minutes and thirteen seconds in 2003.
claims.quote: Cecilia Bartoli, accompagnée par le maestro Myung-Whun Chung a exécuté la danza en seulement deux minutes et treize secondes au cours d'un concert des Victoires de la musique classique en 2003.
